cultivar: Mostly Qingxin; Tieguanyin for aged Muzha tea; occasionally Jin Xuan
processing: Roasted, moderately oxidised oolong (Dong Ding, Hong Shui, Muzha Tieguanyin or Bao Zhong) stored for ten years or more, either re-roasted lightly every few years to keep it dry or sealed in jars and tins and left untouched.
harvest_season: Any; the storage years matter more than the picking season, though the base leaf is usually a spring or winter harvest.
appearance_dry: Dark brown to near-black balls or strips, dull rather than glossy and noticeably light in the hand.
appearance_liquor: Deep reddish-brown to mahogany, clear and bright when the tea has been stored well.
appearance_wet: Leathery dark-brown leaves that open only partly even after many steeps.
taste_profile: Dried plum, dates and old wood with a herbal, medicinal edge and a clean plum-like sourness, thick and smooth, with a sweetness that builds in the throat; mustiness or sharp fire are faults.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, then boiling water in a clay pot; it goes ten or more steeps and very old lots can be simmered after the pot gives out.

vintage_note: Sold by claimed age or decade ('15-year', '1980s Dong Ding'), sometimes with the re-roasting history, and none of it can be proven, so the seller's reputation is the only guarantee; prices climb steeply past twenty years. Most lots on the market are ten to thirty years old and started as roasted Dong Ding, Hong Shui, Muzha Tieguanyin or Bao Zhong; green high-mountain tea is not aged.
description:
Lao cha, 'old tea', is what Taiwan calls oolong that has been kept for ten, twenty or thirty years, and it is a different drink from the fresh, green tea the island is known for: dark, smooth, plummy and slightly sour, closer in spirit to an aged pu-erh than to the Dong Ding or Muzha Tieguanyin it started out as. Most of it was never meant to be aged. It is unsold stock from Lugu, Muzha and Pinglin tea shops that farmers kept rather than dumped, re-roasted now and then to keep it dry, and found decades later to have turned into something worth money.

There are two schools. The traditional one re-roasts the tea lightly every few years, which keeps moisture out but slowly adds roast on top of age; the other seals the tea in jars or tins and leaves it alone, so the change comes only from time and the slow oxidation of what was already in the leaf. Roasted Qing Xin oolong, Hong Shui and Muzha Tieguanyin are the usual starting points because a roasted, moderately oxidised leaf ages gracefully; green high-mountain tea just goes stale.

The prized note is a clean sourness like dried plum, which shows up after about ten years, with dried dates, old wood, a herbal or medicinal edge and a sweetness that builds in the throat. The texture is thick and the cup is calm; there should be no mustiness and no sharp fire. Brew it hot and generously, rinse once, and use a clay pot; it goes ten or more steeps, and old lots can even be simmered after the pot gives out.

It is sold by claimed age or decade, '15-year', '1980s', sometimes with the re-roasting history, and there is no way to prove any of it, so the seller's reputation is everything. Prices climb steeply with age. The common fake is new tea roasted hard and dark to look old: it tastes of char and bitterness rather than plum, and the wet leaf is blackened instead of leathery brown. Start with a ten-year lot in a small quantity before spending on anything older.

If you want to make your own, buy a medium-roast charcoal Dong Ding or a Hong Shui, seal it well and forget it for a decade.
history:
Lao cha is less a named style than a habit of the Taiwanese tea trade: roasted oolong that went unsold was kept, sometimes re-roasted to keep it dry, and turned out years later to have become a different drink. Little is documented about when this began or who first sold old tea as something special, and most of what circulates is the trade's own telling, including its division into re-roasted and sealed storage.

Ages and storage histories are rarely provable, so treat any dated lot as a seller's claim.
